title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The failure here is one of training data acquisition: Suno admitted it trained on essentially all music files available on the internet, including material scraped from YouTube, Deezer, and Genius, without obtaining licenses from rights holders. The consequence visible in the output layer is that the system could reproduce recognizable versions of specific copyrighted songs when prompted with descriptions of genre, decade, and artist style, meaning protected expression was encoded into model weights in a recoverable form. This is a case of a system built on unlicensed data producing output that reproduces characteristics of that data closely enough to constitute alleged infringement under multiple legal frameworks.

The failure would have been catchable at the data-curation stage, before training began, through rights clearance or exclusion of copyrighted material. It was instead surfaced by adversarial prompting from plaintiffs after the system was publicly deployed. A German court ruled against Suno in a case brought by GEMA, and Suno lost a bid to dismiss artists' copyright claims in a separate proceeding, while Warner Music settled its lawsuit and launched a joint venture with the company.

What is not established is that any court has issued a final verdict finding deliberate or willful infringement in the U.S. cases, that all settlements constitute admissions of wrongdoing, or that the damages figures cited in ongoing suits reflect amounts that will ultimately be awarded.

summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records, have filed lawsuits against AI music generators Udio and Suno, claiming the companies scraped thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their models. The labels allege that both companies not only unlawfully copied massive amounts of music but also directly reproduced sections of famous songs in their generated output. The record labels claim the companies have been deliberately secretive about their training data, though both previously argued their use constitutes fair use.

To support their case, the record labels demonstrated they could recreate recognizable versions of famous songs by using targeted prompts describing specific decades, genres, and artist styles. Examples include generating songs mimicking Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode," Green Day's "American Idiot," and Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The lawsuits were filed in New York against Udio and Massachusetts against Suno, and include a list of thousands of copyrighted works the labels claim were scraped, featuring artists like The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, and Bruce Springsteen.
